## Subhead: The GnomeAid 3.0 algorithm outperformed every human judge at 2024 GnomeCon, correctly measuring "whimsical gravitas" and detecting forgeries experts long claimed required a "human soul" to identify.
*DES MOINES, IA —*

Displaced lead appraiser Marnie Huxley, 62, told reporters she’d spent 38 years honing her ability to date a gnome’s weathered patina by the way its ceramic beard fades at the tips, a skill she’d assumed was fully immune to automation.
“I thought we were safe because the job required vibe,” Huxley said. “Turns out the AI can scan a 1-inch tall gnome figurine in 0.2 seconds and tell you what year it was made, how many winters it spent outside in Minnesota, and if its tiny wheelbarrow has enough rust to count as 'vintage charm' vs. 'just damaged.' I’m applying to the local candle shop next. At least candles smell like something a computer can’t do. Probably.”

The Silicon Valley startup behind GnomeAid 3.0, which raised $47 million in seed funding last year, says their algorithm has one remaining flaw: it consistently docks 15 points from any gnome wearing tiny rain boots, a bias traced to a training data set that overrepresented sun-worshipping gnome variants. The team’s next announced project is an AI that can grade middle school science fair volcanoes; they have not yet shared plans to develop AI for healthcare or affordable housing.

Organizers of the annual GnomeCon “Best Dressed Gnome” parade say they’ve already received a formal application from GnomeAid 3.0 to judge 2025’s contest, sparking a petition signed by all 12 remaining human parade judges.
